articles.title: Supreme Court blocks Missouri’s attempt to use newly drawn Republican congressional map
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday blocked an attempt by a Republican state official in Missouri to use a newly drawn GOP congressional map for this year’s elections.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday blocked an attempt by a Republican state official in Missouri to use a newly drawn GOP congressional map for this year’s elections. The court, in a brief order with no noted dissents, granted an emergency request brought by a group called People Not Politicians, led by activist Richard von Glahn. The decision puts on hold a decision by Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark, who ruled on Tuesday that the new map must be used, notwithstanding the Missouri Supreme Court reaching the opposite conclusion. The swift action from the justices likely signals the end of the battle over which congressional map to use in the midterm elections this November, with the state likely to use the previous map from 2022 that includes six seats currently held by Republicans and two held by Democrats. The new map sought to eliminate one of the state’s two Democratic-held seats, currently held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, D-Mo. “The law is the law, the Missouri constitution is clear, as was the Missouri Supreme Court,” von Glahn said in a statement. Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican who led the effort to use the new map, “has shown that he cannot effectively do the job he was elected to do,” he added. Hoskins’ lawyers told the U.S. Supreme Court justices just minutes before the decision was issued that only Clark’s order is “preventing the disenfranchisement of hundreds of thousands of voters” who participated in the primary election using the new congressional map. With little time before the November election, it is the only way that Missouri can “conduct congressional elections that comply with the federal election calendar,” they added. The Trump administration also filed a brief backing Hoskins, saying that if the justices were to block Clark’s ruling, it would “jeopardize state officials’ ability to conduct a timely and lawful federal election.” This is the second time the underlying fight has reached the U.S. Supreme Court. On Tuesday, Justice Brett Kavanaugh rejected a request from Hoskins seeking to block the Missouri Supreme Court ruling. In a separate hearing on Thursday, the Missouri Supreme Court gave Hoskins a cool reception as it considers whether to hold him in contempt for defying its previous ruling. With Hoskins appearing in person, the judges peppered his lawyer with questions about whether he will now comply and use the 2022 map. They seemed dissatisfied with some of the responses. William Seidleck, a lawyer with the Missouri Attorney General’s Office representing Hoskins, said his client would comply with the state court order requiring use of the 2022 map “unless and until” there is an intervening federal court decision. Hoskins is still “evaluating next steps,” he added. Chief Justice Brent Powell told Hoskins not to “venture far from Jefferson City” while the court considers the contempt motion. He also pressed Hoskins to issue updated guidance to local election officials. “We just want to make sure the law is followed,” Powell added. Among his concerns is that if the legal fight continues, it could lead to ongoing issues after the election over whether the congressional delegation should be seated. “We are in a precarious situation,” Powell said. The broader clash is over a congressional map Missouri Republicans enacted in 2025, part of a nationwide redistricting push led by President Donald Trump. The legal fight began when opponents of the new map gathered signatures in support of a state referendum that would undo the GOP-drawn map and put it on hold for the 2026 election. But Hoskins delayed a decision on whether to include the measure on the ballot, waiting to the last minute before rejecting the plan, arguing that redistricting plans are not subject to voters’ approval. The Missouri Supreme Court, which has a majority of Republican appointees, disagreed, saying there was nothing in state law that exempted congressional maps passed by the Legislature from being vetoed by voters via the referendum process. The federal lawsuit was filed by Rick Brattin, the Republican nominee in the district currently held by Cleaver, as well as Rep. Bob Onder, R-Mo. and two voters. Clark then ruled Tuesday that the state must use the map that people voted in during the primary. The drama was playing out even after Tuesday’s deadline to finalize Missouri ballots ahead of this fall’s elections. First ballots are set to go out in the state on Sept. 19.

articles.title: Trump should remove the Iran War’s most dangerous tripwire
articles.summary: The blockade hurts Iran, but it no longer justifies the risks.
articles.body:
The economic warfare against Iran under Operation Economic Outcast runs on two clocks: destroying Iran’s economic timeline and extending the global economic timeline. Further escalation against Iran offers diminishing returns.

The blockade hurts Iran, but it no longer justifies the risks. The more consequential side of the equation is extending the global economic runway by scaling energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz.

The basic premise is that imposing sufficient economic pain on Iran before President Trump is forced to cry uncle could bring about mass uprisings that topple the leadership. That outcome may be unlikely, but it is not impossible.

However, Iran has made clear multiple times that it is adopting a posture that is “offensively defensive.” If sufficient pressure is imposed by the U.S., Tehran will seek to escalate before those uprisings are potentially sparked.

Unfortunately, this runs into the most fundamental problem for the Trump administration in this war: escalation dominance. Iran has shown not just the willingness, but the capability to strike Gulf energy and desalination infrastructure throughout this war. Add to this the well-documented depletion of American interceptor missiles , and it is difficult to credibly assert that the U.S. can reliably prevent such a response from Iran.

If sufficient economic pressures are imposed upon Iran, they will certainly pull the lever of targeting Gulf infrastructure, even if that significantly deteriorates relations with neighboring countries. This is an existential war. But before pursuing that avenue, Iran may determine that striking American forces offers a more justified escalation pathway that avoids deteriorating relations with their Gulf neighbors.

Iran may therefore seek to target the U.S. warships imposing the blockade instead as an eventual step up the escalation ladder. Just this past weekend, U.S. Central Command acknowledged that Iran had targeted two American warships with ballistic missiles, forcing both to make evasive maneuvers.

Whether or not the blockade remains, Iran retains the ability to escalate against Gulf infrastructure. It does, however, provide Tehran with an additional and potentially appealing escalation pathway: striking American vessels or troops in the region. One successful strike on a U.S. warship could produce an American mass casualty event. Thousands more Americans remain exposed at bases in Jordan , despite limited benefit to the economic warfare campaign at this scale.

At that point, Trump’s political calculus changes entirely. The question is no longer whether Washington should escalate. It becomes whether an American president can politically afford not to. That is how another Middle Eastern forever war begins.

The blockade also fails under either possible strategic scenario. If Project Freedom — created to get commercial ships safely through the Strait of Hormuz — cannot extend the global economic runway beyond Iran’s economic runway, then Washington will run out of time before economic pressure produces the political rupture it seeks. The blockade cannot fix that.

But if Project Freedom can extend the global runway long enough for Iran’s economy to reach a breaking point, then the blockade is no longer necessary to preserve that pathway. Sanctions, financial isolation and accumulated wartime destruction can continue to maintain the terminal tailspin while the global economy is kept alive.

In neither scenario does the blockade solve Iran’s ability to retaliate across the Gulf. It only adds another target set: American forces.

By removing the U.S. blockade, the Iranian economy does not magically undo the roughly hundred billion dollars in damages suffered during the U.S. bombing campaign. It does not erase the losses imposed by two iterations of the blockade. And it certainly does not reopen the economic escape valves Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is seeking to shut through Operation Economic Outcast.

Prior to the Iran War, Iran’s economy was already in atrocious condition. Since the war began, inflation has continued to skyrocket . The Rial has fallen to 2.2 million per dollar, and intensified U.S. sanctions have further constrained Tehran’s ability to relieve that pressure.

The war did not create Iran’s economic crisis. It deepened it. Removing the blockade may slow the deterioration, but it does not stop the clock.

Paired with the American focus on scaling and maintaining navigation along the Omani coastline under Project Freedom, the Trump administration can still seek to extend the global economic runway beyond Iran’s economic runway. Whether the U.S. is moving 8 million barrels per day along this route or 10 million , the strategic objective is the same: to buy more time.

The U.S. doesn’t need to make Iran collapse faster by accepting potentially catastrophic risk. It needs to make the global economy last longer than Iran can. If sufficient economic pressure ultimately forces Tehran to escalate against Gulf infrastructure, that option exists regardless of whether the blockade is maintained. Washington cannot solve Iran’s escalation dominance by keeping American ships in place. It can, however, remove unnecessary escalation pathways.

The blockade does not solve the equation. It merely accelerates Iran’s slide toward the point at which it may decide to retaliate, while simultaneously exposing American forces to the most dangerous forms that retaliation could take.

Washington cannot eliminate Iran’s escalation dominance. It can, however, eliminate the risks from the blockade and reduce unnecessary American force posture.

Brett Erickson is managing principal at Obsidian Risk Advisors and an advisory board member at Seton Hall School of Diplomacy and International Relations and DePaul University Driehaus College of Business.

articles.title: Who is Trump trying to exclude from 2030 US census and why does it matter?
articles.summary: Census plan would exclude undocumented immigrants and non-green-card holders, deeming them not ‘true inhabitants’.
articles.body:
The administration of United States President Donald Trump has released a proposal to remove millions of non-US citizens from national census data.

The plan to exclude non-citizens and those who are not permanent residents from the next full census in 2030 could have dramatic implications for federal aid and political representation, analysts say.

The proposal comes amid the Trump administration’s broader immigration crackdown and efforts to reshape electoral power, including through congressional redistricting and restrictions on mail-in voting , which activists say could disenfranchise minorities.

Here’s what we know about the census proposal and the potential political effects:

A memo from the Department of Commerce on Wednesday proposes that only US citizens and permanent residents should be counted in the national census.

That would exclude undocumented immigrants, as well as other lawful temporary immigrants who do not have a green card, which is issued to permanent residents.

The department has justified the proposal by saying undocumented immigrants and other foreigners without a durable legal status are not “true inhabitants” and lack a sufficient “tie and allegiance” to the US.

The proposal also suggests eliminating some questions on race and ethnicity, which have been part of the questionnaire since 1790, as well as a question on sexual orientation.

The proposal is open for a 30-day public comment period, then the commerce department will review feedback before setting any new policy.

Trump has long called for a change in census policy, writing on his Truth Social platform last year that “people who are in our country illegally will not be counted”.

According to the US Constitution, Congress has ultimate say over the census.

How many would be left out after census change?

The Pew Research Center estimated there were 14 million undocumented immigrants in the US in 2023, the last year it shows data for. It estimated there were at least two million more immigrants in the US lawfully but without permanent status – they would also be excluded under the proposed change.

More than half of undocumented immigrants in the US were concentrated in just six states in 2023 – California, Texas, Florida, New York, New Jersey and Illinois – according to Pew.

California had the highest number, with an estimated 2.3 million, followed by Texas with 2.1 million.

What impact could it have on federal resources?

The Census Bureau says its data informs the direction of hundreds of billions of dollars in federal funding annually, including money allocated to schools, hospitals and public infrastructure.

Rights advocates say excluding undocumented immigrants and lawful temporary immigrants from the count could distort the data, potentially underfunding cities or states with high immigrant populations.

Meeta Anand, senior director of the census and data ⁠⁠equity programme at the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights, told Reuters the effect could be “earth-shattering”.

Census data “undergirds so ⁠⁠much of our democracy and our society,” Anand said. “So you’ll start seeing a very inaccurate picture of our country and then we’re making political decisions, business decisions, investment decisions based on data that are flawed.”

What could it mean for political representation?

It could alter representation in Congress and the electoral college as well.

The US uses census data to decide how many seats each state is allocated in the House of Representatives, as well as how to draw up electoral districts to ensure that representation is largely equal across the whole country.

As a result, areas with high undocumented immigrant populations could lose representation. In addition, states which lose House seats could lose votes in the electoral college , which decides the presidency.

Critics say the Trump administration’s census proposal flouts the 14th Amendment to the Constitution, which states that political representatives should be based on “the ‌‌whole number of persons in each State”.

New York Attorney General Letitia James said that her office was looking into ways to legally challenge the census plan. “The Constitution is clear. Every person living in the United States, regardless of immigration status, must be counted in the census,” she posted on X.

The Center for American Progress, a liberal public policy institute, called the proposal “a flagrant assault on our democracy, designed to manipulate voting maps and dilute the political representation of diverse American communities”.

It urged citizens to petition their representatives to oppose the policy, which would not come into effect until after Trump leaves office.

articles.title: Jimmy Kimmel says show won’t air James Talarico interview on TV, citing FCC threats
articles.summary: Jimmy Kimmel announced on Wednesday night that his show would not air his upcoming interview with Texas’ Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico on television, citing the Trump administration’s threats against ABC.
articles.body: Jimmy Kimmel announced on Wednesday night that his show would not air his upcoming interview with Texas’ Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico on television, citing the Trump administration’s threats against ABC. Kimmel said that during President Donald Trump’s administration, the Federal Communications Commission “has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple, traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don’t like.” “Out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas, who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television,” he said. The interview, set for Thursday, will be posted on the YouTube channel for “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” instead, he said. Talarico, a Democratic state representative in Texas, is locked in a competitive Senate race with Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton. The Talarico campaign and the FCC did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment. ABC Entertainment declined to comment. FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, condemned “FCC intimidation” in a statement reacting to Kimmel’s announcement. “No host, local affiliate, or network should have to weigh federal retaliation before booking a guest for a newsworthy interview,” Gomez said in the statement. “Any attempt to pressure broadcasters into self-censorship undermines both press freedom and the public’s right to hear from candidates in their communities seeking public office.” Kimmel’s announcement marks the latest apparent instance in which pressure from the administration has affected content aired on an entertainment show. Stephen Colbert said in February that CBS did not air his interview with Talarico out of fear of the FCC. “He was supposed to be here, but we were told in no uncertain terms by our network’s lawyers, who called us directly, that we could not have him on the broadcast,” Colbert said at the time. CBS said in a February statement that “the show was provided legal guidance that the broadcast could trigger the FCC equal-time rule for two other candidates.” Trump has publicly targeted Kimmel in the past, calling multiple times for the comedian to be fired. About a year ago, ABC pulled Kimmel’s show following the comedian’s comments about conservative activist Charlie Kirk, who was assassinated in September of last year. The show returned nearly a week later, and Kimmel said in his monologue that “it was never my intention to make light of the murder of a young man.” The FCC, under Chairman Brendan Carr, announced in April that Disney’s eight local television stations owned and operated by ABC needed to file broadcast license renewals early. The Walt Disney Co. sued over the decision last month. In January, the FCC issued a memo saying that late-night and daytime talk shows must adhere to the equal time rule, which requires broadcasters to offer equal opportunities to other qualified candidates who are running for the same office. The memo marked a change in the FCC’s position. Twenty years earlier, a decision found that late-night and daytime talk shows were exempt from the rule. Trump himself was interviewed by Kimmel in 2015, when he was running for president. Kimmel recalled the interview during his Wednesday show. “At that time, when he was the one sitting next to me, he seemed to have no problem with the idea of talk show hosts interviewing candidates,” he said. “In fact, he was very eager to come back for another interview, which he did just before he became the nominee in 2016.” “But for some reason, and I can’t seem to figure out what that reason is, something has changed,” he said, tongue in cheek.

articles.title: Trump administration keeps TPS in place for El Salvador for now
articles.summary: The Trump administration has not said whether it will let deportation protections lapse for Salvadoran nationals in the U.S. — a different track after the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) ended Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for 13 other countries. The department on Wednesday said TPS would remain in effect for El Salvador, a country led…
articles.body:
The Trump administration has not said whether it will let deportation protections lapse for Salvadoran nationals in the U.S. — a different track after the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) ended Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for 13 other countries.

The department on Wednesday said TPS would remain in effect for El Salvador, a country led by Trump ally Nayib Bukele, who last year agreed to imprison U.S. deportees in exchange for millions of dollars from the administration.

“An announcement on El Salvador’s TPS will be made at the appropriate time. Until such announcement is made, Salvadoran individuals present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection,” DHS said in a statement.

DHS has not always immediately announced decisions on how it will handle expiring TPS programs, but it has fought aggressively in court to end the program, arguing that the temporary protections must be temporary.

The Supreme Court earlier this year determined the courts did not have the power to review the administration’s decision, allowing for the end of TPS for some 350,000 Haitians.

In addition to El Salvador, just three other countries have TPS protections that will soon expire: Sudan, Ukraine and Lebanon.

TPS allows nationals from a designated country to remain in the U.S. if it’s determined that unrest or natural disasters would make it unsafe to conduct deportations.

Haiti appears to clearly meet the parameters of the program, as the U.S. currently does not allow commercial flights into the country as gangs routinely shoot at planes. The country has remained in a transitional government since the 2021 assassination of its prime minister.

El Salvador shares characteristics with other countries the Trump administration has determined no longer qualify for TPS.

TPS for El Salvador was first established in 2001 after two massive earthquakes, and 170,000 people currently hold the protections.

The Biden administration extended the protections just days before the end of its term.

“While progress has been made in repairing physical damage caused by the 2001 earthquakes, subsequent environmental disasters, infrastructure challenges, continued climate risks, a weak macroeconomic environment, and food insecurity underscore that the country conditions underlying the original designation continue to significantly disrupt living conditions in El Salvador,” DHS wrote at the time.

The Trump administration ended TPS for other countries in the same region that were also struck by natural disasters, ending the protections for Nicaragua and Honduras, which were both designated in the wake of Hurricane Mitch in 1999.

Bukele has been a top ally of President Trump, accepting both Salvadoran and Venezuelan deportees and holding them in one of the country’s most notorious megaprisons.

He has also touted the security of an El Salvador previously marred by violence, a dynamic achieved after imprisoning tens of thousands of Salvadorans.

articles.title: Fox News’s Baier presses Vance on Trump’s $5K dividend promise
articles.summary: Fox News anchor Bret Baier pressed Vice President Vance on President Trump’s pledge to give Americans $5,000 if Republicans keep control of Congress come November, saying critics would respond to the roughly $1.3 trillion payout as “bribing voters.” “I can hear the critics’ heads exploding,” Baier told Vance late Wednesday, hours after Trump made the…
articles.body:
Fox News anchor Bret Baier pressed Vice President Vance on President Trump’s pledge to give Americans $5,000 if Republicans keep control of Congress come November, saying critics would respond to the roughly $1.3 trillion payout as “bribing voters.”

“I can hear the critics’ heads exploding,” Baier told Vance late Wednesday, hours after Trump made the vow on the first night of the GOP midterm convention in Dallas.

“They’re saying out loud, I guarantee you: ‘The president is bribing voters to vote for Republicans to take over the House, and then he’s bankrupting the country because the deficit and debt is huge and inflation would come back if this comes into play,’” the host added.

Vance defended the proposal, calling the payments a “dividend for American workers.”

“We’re taking an extraordinary amount of revenue,” he said, referring to the revenue generated by Trump’s tariffs , which he said Americans should receive a share of. The administration previously floated $2,000 tariff dividends .

“If you keep us in power and allow us to continue to do these things, then you’re going to share in some of the benefit of this incredible wealth that we’re creating in the United States of America,” the vice president continued. “I don’t think it’s a controversial idea.”

Trump announced the proposal during his nearly two-hour speech , saying he would issue a $5,000 “dividend” to every adult U.S. citizen if Republicans maintain majorities in the House and Senate in November.

“Because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” the president told the crowd.

He also said the money would need to be spent domestically but did not provide details.

“We don’t want you going to Canada to spend the money,” Trump added. “We don’t want you going to China, to Germany.”

Congress would need to approve the payment, and with roughly 270 million adults in the U.S., sending each of them $5,000 would cost more than $1 trillion. U.S. tariff revenue would also fall short of covering the full cost of the payments as the president described them, according to The Associated Press.

articles.title: Supreme Court blocks Missouri’s use of GOP-favored congressional map
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Thursday blocked an order that told Missouri to keep implementing Republicans’ favored 7-1 congressional map, which sparked confusion about what boundaries would be used in the November election. By lifting that federal judge’s directive, it leaves in place a state court directive that tells elections officials to return to the existing…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court on Thursday blocked an order that told Missouri to keep implementing Republicans’ favored 7-1 congressional map, which sparked confusion about what boundaries would be used in the November election.

By lifting that federal judge’s directive, it leaves in place a state court directive that tells elections officials to return to the existing map with a 6-2 split. The GOP had pushed for a pickup opportunity as part of the mid-decade redistricting war.

Missouri state leaders have said reverting would cause chaos, as they already conducted their primaries using the new map.

The Supreme Court did not publicly explain its decision, and no justice publicly noted a dissent.

Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway’s (R) office warned the justices that blocking the map “would jeopardize Missouri’s ability to hold a timely election.”

“It would disenfranchise hundreds of thousands of Missourians who voted in the Primary. It would force election officials across the State to scramble,” her office wrote in court papers filed minutes earlier. “It would render political campaigns over the past year pointless. And it would leave all Missourians doubting the integrity of their elections.”

It marked the second round at the Supreme Court in less than a week for Missouri’s redistricting battle after the state’s top court ruled Republicans’ favored 7-1 map could not go into effect yet.

That state court’s decision instructed officials to return to the existing design, finding the Missouri Constitution allows a referendum organizer to put the new map to voters before it goes into effect.

But in a separate lawsuit, filed in federal court, a judge told state officials they should still move ahead with their new 7-1 map to avoid widespread voter confusion.

The competing rulings led to public confusion and rapid maneuvers in multiple courts to seek clarity. A contempt hearing is scheduled to take place in Missouri’s top court later Thursday morning.

As Missouri officials vowed to implement Republicans’ favored map, the referendum organizer quickly brought it to the justices in the nation’s capital, seeking an emergency intervention.

In his application filed a day earlier, he called the directive “legally baseless.”

Justice Brett Kavanaugh, an appointee of President Trump who by default manages emergency matters arising from Missouri, declined to get involved in the earlier state court case.

The new federal case raises distinct issues. This time, Kavanaugh referred it to the full court for a vote.

“Missouri Republicans have played their last card, and they lost,” Elias Law Group partner Abha Khanna, who represents the organizer, said in a statement. “Despite increasingly desperate tactics that threatened to throw this November’s election into chaos and drew a strong rebuke from the Missouri Supreme Court, it is now clear after two rejections from the U.S. Supreme Court that Missouri will not be allowed to ram through an egregious gerrymander before the voters have a say.”

Missouri warned the justices against intervening, arguing the referendum organizer has no legal standing to appeal and his arguments are legally meritless. They got the support of the Trump administration, which filed a written brief supporting the state.

“Applicants do not contest that—if Missouri’s congressional map changes—hundreds of thousands of Missourians will vote for candidates in the General Election that they never considered in the Primary Election,” the state wrote.

“Nor could they. That is exactly what they demand.”

John Fetterman is still an embarrassment. The Pennsylvania Democrat enjoys one of the cushiest jobs in America, but he can’t perform basic duties…
articles.body:
The Philadelphia Inquirer editorial board went after Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) following recent reporting on the senator’s work habits and his video appearance at the GOP’s midterm convention.

“News flash: U.S. Sen. John Fetterman is still an embarrassment. The Pennsylvania Democrat enjoys one of the cushiest jobs in America, but he can’t perform basic duties like voting, attending committee hearings, or meeting with constituents,” the board wrote in a piece published Thursday .

In the last few years, Fetterman has increasingly bucked his party, expressed a strongly pro-Israel stance amid tension in the Middle East and gone after the Democratic Party’s left flank, especially democratic socialists.

Fetterman has dismissed what he referred to as “smears” and “half-truths” in a recent Wall Street Journal report, which featured allegations that he dodged constituents and prioritized cozying up to conservative news outlets.

“Per usual — lies, half-truths, innuendos, smears and anonymous,” Fetterman said in a Sunday statement obtained by CNN, later adding, “No matter how many smears or stories, I’m proud to continue to deliver for Pennsylvania.”

Former staffers told the Journal that they believe Fetterman displays a lack of interest in his job besides “cultivating relationships with conservative media figures and advocating for Israel.”

“Apparently, teachers, healthcare officials, police, and veterans take a backseat while Fox News and the Israel-Hamas war command Fetterman’s full attention,” the Inquirer’s editorial board wrote in its Wednesday piece.

“The senator has appeared on the conservative news outlet roughly 60 times this year and has gone on two junkets to Israel since 2024,” the piece continued. “(He even made a cameo at the GOP convention in Dallas Wednesday night to praise Trump and boost Republicans before the midterms.)”

Fetterman on Wednesday appeared in a video praising fellow Pennsylvania Sen. Dave McCormick (R) at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention.

“Why am I here talking to you today?” Fetterman said in a prerecorded video. “Because, well, I’m a commonsense Democrat.”

“David McCormick is the kind of senator that gets the job done,” he added.

The Hill has reached out to Fetterman’s office for comment.

articles.title: Extradition is becoming a political football — here’s how the states can stop it
articles.summary: A governor who wants to shield someone from a prosecution he objects to, or from a sister state whose politics he finds distasteful, may simply keep an extradition demand “under investigation” indefinitely.
articles.body:
The Extradition Clause of the Constitution was designed so that one state’s criminal charges could not be nullified by another state’s politics. But last month’s ruling in the extradition dispute between Texas and Minnesota shows how easy it is to do exactly that.

A governor who wants to shield someone from a prosecution he objects to, or from a sister state whose politics he finds distasteful, may simply keep an extradition demand “under investigation” indefinitely. This is actually just one of many loopholes in extradition law increasingly likely to be exploited in today’s intensely polarized political climate. Texas, Minnesota and the rest of the states can and should seal these legal cracks before they cause further damage to interstate relations and the rule of law.

In late August, Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. declined to order the extradition of Christian Castro, an ICE officer wanted in Minnesota for allegedly shooting Julio Sosa-Celis through a closed door and then lying to investigators about the incident.

Rodriguez’s opinion highlighted a paradox in extradition law: In response to Minnesota’s lawsuit, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) claimed he had not yet decided whether or not to reject Minnesota’s extradition demand — that he was still investigating it. Since Texas said it was still investigating, Rodriguez concluded, the case was not yet ripe for judicial intervention.

However, in a conspicuous footnote, the judge asserted that the answer to the question Texas purported to be investigating — whether as a legal matter Castro qualifies as a “fugitive” from Minnesota — is obviously yes.

So what are we waiting for? How long would this pointless “investigation” have to go on before the law considers it tantamount to a denial?

The answer, Rodriguez rightly points out, is that nobody knows. The Supreme Court has never taken up the issue. Nor will they have the opportunity to do so in Castro’s case, because the federal government recently indicted him , rendering the Minnesota-Texas lawsuit moot. Yet it remains the case that a governor might forestall an extradition indefinitely by claiming to have a perpetually open “investigation.”

My research identifies several other equally vulnerable loopholes in extradition doctrine. If a governor wanted to, he or she could exploit each of these, one at a time. Even if the Supreme Court were to reject each one in turn, the litigation could forestall an extradition for years, even decades.

The Castro case makes clear that this is not a matter of speculation. Americans are intensely polarized on what they consider criminal. Today’s extradition controversy concerned an ICE agent. We narrowly avoided another one in 2023, when Florida Gov. Ron Desantis (R) announced he would not extradite Donald Trump to face criminal charges in New York. (Trump ended up voluntarily surrendering himself .)

The next conflict might involve a father who took his child out of state for gender-affirming care. The one after that could be a doctor who performed an abortion she viewed as medically necessary but was prohibited under state law. How about a reviled former FBI director indicted on charges that are flimsy and obviously pretextual ?

Abbott showed that governors faced with extradition demands of this nature will not hesitate to exploit gaps in the law to block or delay an uncomfortable extradition. And as the examples above illustrate, extradition conflicts do not have an inherent left-right political valence.

It is in all of the states’ interests to fix this mess. Fortunately, they can.

The principle that states must extradite fugitives wanted for trial in other states comes from the Constitution’s Extradition Clause . But that clause, and the related federal Extradition Act , are notoriously vague. In the 1920s and 1930s, states joined together to fill in cracks that had emerged over the previous 150 years. They came up with the Uniform Criminal Extradition Act , a set of laws adopted by 48 states and still in place to this day.

One hundred years later, it is time for the states to take initiative once again. They may decide to seal up the loopholes and require extradition under all circumstances. Or they may decide to expressly permit governors to refuse extradition in extraordinary cases.

I prefer the latter resolution. I believe that preventing an escalation in political prosecutions is worth the cost of a few going free who deserve punishment. This was, incidentally, the state of affairs for almost 200 years before a landmark Supreme Court case in 1987 . And it is how the states decided to handle cases like extraterritorial crimes that fall outside of the Constitution’s Extradition Clause.

Still, I would happily accept the certainty of either option over the ambiguity we have now. Texas may enjoy its victory for the moment, but it will inevitably find itself in Minnesota’s shoes before long. It is in every state’s interest, and every American’s interest, to close the many loopholes in extradition law.

Ethan Lowens is a research fellow at the Quattrone Center for the Administration of Justice at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School.

articles.title: Supreme Court again blocks Missouri from using Trump-backed congressional maps
articles.summary: The Supreme Court blocked Missouri's Republican-backed congressional map for a second time as a contempt hearing looms for Denny Hoskins this week.
articles.body: The Supreme Court turned back another effort to use Missouri congressional maps supported by President Donald Trump. "The application for stay presented to Justice [Brett] Kavanaugh and by him referred to the Court is granted," Thursday's ruling read. The court's brief order was unsigned and gave no explanation, as is common when the justices handle emergency matters. No justice publicly dissented from the decision. MISSOURI AG FILES PETITION ASKING SUPREME COURT TO REVIVE TRUMP-BACKED REDISTRICTING MAP While the Missouri Supreme Court’s ruling paved the way for use of the old maps, the state’s Aug. 4 primary was already held under the new maps. "After repeated legal victories defending Missouri’s fair and lawful map, this 11th-hour ruling pulls the rug out from under voters who already cast their primary ballots," RNC Election Integrity Communications Director Ally Triolo wrote in a statement. "Changing the rules mid-election is reckless and wrong." The court’s decision came after U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark ordered Missouri to use the new map, conflicting with a unanimous ruling by the Missouri Supreme Court that said the districts had not legally taken effect and that the state’s older map should be used unless voters approve the changes. Republican state officials have argued it would violate voters' federal rights to switch districts before the general election. MISSOURI HIGH COURT BLOCKS GOP-BACKED CONGRESSIONAL MAPS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS; TRUMP BLASTS 'RIDICULOUS' RULING The Missouri Supreme Court also ordered Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins to appear at a contempt hearing Thursday, after he instructed local election officials to use the new districts. A federal judge declined to halt that hearing before the Supreme Court issued its order. The redrawn map was approved by Missouri Republicans in 2025. It dismantles the Kansas City-based 5th Congressional District held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, D-Mo., by shifting portions of the seat into neighboring districts and extending the remainder into heavily Republican areas. The way the map was designed gave Republicans a strong chance of winning seven of Missouri’s eight House seats, compared with the current six-to-two Republican advantage. Opponents of the map, including the group People Not Politicians, submitted hundreds of thousands of petition signatures seeking a statewide referendum. The Missouri Supreme Court ordered that referendum to appear on the November ballot, meaning voters will decide whether the redrawn map can be used in future elections. articles.title: 9/11 hero’s memory preserved through massive effort to ‘do good’ for vets, first responders: ‘His legacy’
articles.summary: Tunnel to Towers' 343 Homes Initiative honors Stephen Siller and the 9/11 firefighters with mortgage-free homes for fallen first responders' families.
articles.body: On one of the darkest days in America’s history, New York City firefighter Stephen Siller strapped on his gear and ran through the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel to the collapsing Twin Towers, ultimately giving his life to save those caught in the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. Two and a half decades later, Tunnel to Towers, founded by Siller’s family, has continued his legacy through its commitment to "do good" for veterans and first responders and their families across the country. Since its founding, inspired by Siller and his favorite quote, "While we have time, let us do good," Tunnel to Towers has provided more than 1,700 mortgage-free homes to the families of fallen service members and first responders, as well as to disabled veterans and first responders. The organization has also delivered housing assistance and support services to more than 20,000 homeless veterans and holds hundreds of events nationwide to honor America’s heroes and preserve the memory of those who lost their lives for future generations. Tunnel to Towers CEO Frank Siller, the brother of the 34-year-old firefighter who gave his life on Sept. 11, previously warned in 2020 that America was "very close to forgetting the impact 9/11 had on our nation." Now, with anti-American sentiment on the rise and some online commentators belittling the Sept. 11 attacks or even justifying them, many worry the legacy of those who lost their lives, including the 343 members of the New York City Fire Department who made the ultimate sacrifice, will be forgotten. Siller, however, has vowed that "Tunnel to Towers will never let that happen." 9/11 IS BECOMING HISTORY. MY GENERATION MUST MAKE SURE AMERICA NEVER FORGETS The Tunnel to Towers 9/11 Institute has helped to educate students from kindergarten through 12th grade on the "extraordinary heroism and goodness of everyday people" on Sept. 11, "while demonstrating the strength and resilience of America’s spirit." Its mobile 9/11 exhibit has traveled to nearly all 50 states as well as Canada. This year, Tunnel to Towers launched its "Steel Across America" display, in which a 16,000-pound steel beam pulled from the wreckage of the World Trade Center traveled more than 10,500 miles to 35 stops across 21 states and the District of Columbia, culminating in New York City. articles.title: Chip Roy on Trump dividends: ‘Dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms’
articles.summary: Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) criticized President Trump’s Wednesday proposal to give every American adult a $5,000 dividend if the GOP wins the midterms, as other Republicans have also voiced skepticism about the pledge. “Some of us think dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms,” Roy wrote Thursday on social platform X, pushing back…
articles.body:
Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) criticized President Trump’s Wednesday proposal to give every American adult a $5,000 dividend if the GOP wins the midterms, as other Republicans have also voiced skepticism about the pledge.

“Some of us think dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms,” Roy wrote Thursday on social platform X , pushing back on venture capitalist Clint Brown’s defense of the president’s proposal .

On Wednesday, the staunchly conservative Texan estimated that giving every American adult $5,000 would cost the federal government $1.2 trillion in fiscal 2027.

“Dear certain friends… deficits aside – you could almost ZERO out taxes for married parents of dependents up to $200,000 over 10 years!” Roy wrote on X .

Trump made the promise Wednesday, saying he will send the dividends to every adult citizen only if Republicans maintain control of the House and Senate in November.

“Because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” he said at the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas.

There are roughly 270 million adults in the U.S. The president did not offer specifics on the proposal outside of saying recipients could only spend the money in the U.S.

“We don’t want you going to Canada to spend the money,” Trump remarked. “We don’t want you going to China, to Germany.”

It is unclear whether Congress would have to pass legislation approving the dividends. When the president proposed sending $2,000 tariff dividend checks to Americans last year, he claimed he didn’t “believe” he needed congressional approval to do so. The tariff dividend checks proposal never came to fruition.

Trump made Wednesday’s promise less than a month after the U.S. national debt crossed the $40 trillion threshold . The debt has increased by more than $3.8 trillion since the start of the president’s second term.

Roy’s estimated cost of the dividend is slightly less than the amount the federal government has paid in interest on the debt this fiscal year: $1.27 trillion . The U.S. government has paid more than $1 trillion in interest on the debt in each of the last three fiscal years.

Roy, who is departing Congress after losing the GOP primary runoff for Texas attorney general in May, was not alone among Republicans in opposing Trump’s proposal.

Former Rep. Bob Good (R-Va.) called the idea a “socialist vote-buying scheme” early Thursday morning.

“Sadly, most ‘conservatives’ don’t even know (or care) that the president doesn’t have the constitutional authority to spend $$, or send out ‘dividend’ checks without Congress,” Good wrote later Thursday on X .

articles.title: Denver sues to block ICE officers from voting sites
articles.summary: The city of Denver filed a lawsuit Thursday to block Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers from going to voting sites. The lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Secretary Markwayne Mullin argues that ordering federal officers to carry out detainments and serve warrants violated the “troops at polls” law. The troops at…
articles.body:
The city of Denver filed a lawsuit Thursday to block Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers from going to voting sites.

The lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Secretary Markwayne Mullin argues that ordering federal officers to carry out detainments and serve warrants violated the “troops at polls” law.

The troops at polls law , established by Congress during the Civil War, imposed fines and potential jail time for federal officers who show up to “any place where a general or special election is held, unless such force be necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.”

The lawyers for Denver and other plaintiffs — including immigrant rights groups League of United Latin American Citizens, Common Cause and UnidosUS — wrote, “the specter of armed officers at polling places threatens the freedom of this upcoming election.”

“It places voters in fear that they will be confronted by armed federal immigration enforcement officers if they choose to cast a ballot,” they continued.

Mullin clarified on Sept. 1 that his policy would only order ICE officers to appear at polling places “if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down.”

The plaintiffs pushed back on this claim, citing violent encounters with officers over the past year — notably two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who were killed in separate incidents in January.

They also cited a ProPublica report that alleged ICE had detained more than 170 U.S. citizens in the first nine months of President Trump’s second term.

“DHS Defendants’ failure to engage in reasoned decision making and disregard for existing federal law taints the Polling Place Policy,” they wrote.

Denver Mayor Mike Johnston wrote in a statement Thursday that stationing ICE officers near voting sites “is only meant to scare people and suppress votes.”

“We’ll fight tooth and nail to prevent it,” he said.

UnidosUS President and CEO Janet Murguía similarly called the move by ICE “voter suppression plain and simple.”

The lawsuit comes amid concerns from Democrats about federal government officials having a presence at voting sites during this year’s midterm elections.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has plans to deploy monitors to voting sites this November, and The Hill’s sister network NewsNation reports that the DOJ deployed monitors in Rhode Island Wednesday during the Ocean State’s primary election.

The Trump administration is also pursuing restrictions on mail-in voting and creating voter lists alongside the added ICE security — though the window to implement these rules is closing as Election Day is about two months away.

ICE did not respond to The Hill’s request for immediate comment.

articles.title: House ‘member day’ hearing airs reform proposals
articles.summary: The House Rules Committee recently held its biennial hearing where 12 members provided recommendations ranging from remote proxy voting for parents to improved legislative time allocation and stricter ethics enforcement.
articles.body:
Last Wednesday, the House Rules Committee held its biennial hearing for members to make recommendations for changes in House rules they hope to see adopted in the next Congress.

Twelve members testified — ten Democrats, one Republican, and one independent. Their recommendations ranged from remote proxy voting for parents of newborns, to stricter ethics enforcement rules and better allocations of time for legislating.

The tradition of holding such House reform hearings in every even-numbered year originated in the 104th Congress (1995-96) when Republicans regained majority party status for the first time in 40 years. The Republican “Contract with America” promised not only to pass major policy changes in the first 100-days of the new Congress but also to adopt nine significant House rules changes.

These included such significant alterations as placing term limits on Speakers and committee chairs, abolishing proxy voting in committee, and reducing the number of committees and cutting committee staff by one-third. Also agreed to were 23 minor revisions, including requiring committees to adopt oversight agendas at the beginning of each Congress and limiting members to no more than two full committee and four subcommittee assignments.

The precedent for member day reform hearings was established in the 104th Congress when Rules Committee Chairman Gerald Solomon (R-N.Y.) launched an unprecedented bipartisan process for his committee to take input from members and outside experts to build on changes made in the 104th Congress and preparing for the 105th. It began with a “Members’ Open Day” hearing on July 17, 1996.

In Solomon’s words , “We’re still committed to changing the way Congress does business.” He added that “many members have good ideas on how to conduct the people’s business more efficiently and we’re going to give them a good look.” That initial members’ day hearing heard from 16 members, six Republicans and ten Democrats. Recommendations included ways to improve civility in the House and modifications in ethics rules.

In the 105th Congress (1997-98), the Rules Committee conducted its second ever “Open Day” hearing for members on Sept. 17, 1998. It sought proposals for changes in the House Rules for the 106th Congress. Many of the previous House rules changes were incorporated in a total recodification of House rules on opening day of the106th Congress, while still paring the number of rules from 52 to 28.

Last week’s members’ day hearing elicited an interesting variety of proposals, the main focus of which seemed to be how to better allocate members’ time, both in Washington and in their home districts. Rep. Chrissy Houlahan (D-Pa.) called for “better and longer” district work periods. Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) suggested the House work a full, five-day work week, with one of the five days devoted solely to committee work to allow more time for committee interaction, and that the work weeks alternate with a full district week.

Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) urged that daycare be given a higher priority; that rural districts be given greater access and exposure through remote hearings; and that when members are not able to perform their duties, the House be allowed a way to address that situation.

It is difficult to gauge the utility of these member day hearings. They provide an occasion for members to vent frustrations. Perhaps that alone is sufficient justification for their existence. Understandably, the minority party has more reasons to vent and more ideas for how to give it fairer treatment, given the majority’s overwhelming procedural advantages in the House.

Although the Rules Committee does not even exist in a new Congress until the standing rules are adopted on opening day, its members do have significant input in the rules proposed by the majority party caucus. The bipartisan sympathy for parents of newborns, for instance, could result in limited proxy floor voting in such circumstances. The same goes for stricter conflict of interest rules barring insider stock and prediction market trading.

To summarize the general attitude of those members who have bothered to think about and testify on how to make the House a better place in which to serve, there is a feeling that legislators are spread too thinly to give necessary attention to their committee, floor and district responsibilities.

That may sound like a self-serving defense by members asking for greater comfort and convenience. For the most part, though, it is a sincere desire to serve their constituents in a more reliable and conscientious manner. Given the public’s current low-level of regard for Congress, it should appreciate such high-minded endeavors to improve the institution’s behavior and performance.

Don Wolfensberger is a 28-year congressional staff veteran who served as as chief of staff of the House Rules Committee. He is author of “Congress and the People: Deliberative Democracy on Trial,” and, “Changing Cultures in Congress: From Fair Play to Power Plays.”

articles.title: UN expert Albanese, protesters warn against Italy’s anti-Semitism bill
articles.summary: Protesters in Rome and UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese, warn proposed law could silence criticism of Israel.
articles.body:
Rome, Italy – “Anti-Zionism is not anti-Semitism”, read the black-and-yellow signs distributed by Amnesty International outside the Italian parliament on Wednesday afternoon.

Hundreds gathered in front of Montecitorio Square in Rome to oppose Italy’s so-called anti-Semitism bill.

The demonstration was organised to coincide with a meeting of the Chamber of Deputies’ Constitutional Affairs Committee, which is examining legislation approved by the Senate on March 4 by a large majority. Under Italy’s constitutional system, a bill must be approved by both chambers in the same text before it can become law.

“We are tired of seeing anti-Semitism instrumentalised to promote censorship of any kind of criticism of the State of Israel and its criminal policies,” said Daniel Calo, of Tikkun, a group of Italian Jewish antiracism activists.

“In the face of this shameful bill, we reiterate once again, forcefully, that opposing Zionism is not anti-Semitism.”

At the centre of the controversy is the possible adoption into national law of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s ( IHRA ) definition of anti-Semitism, which critics argue conflates anti-Semitism with criticism of Israel.

According to the IHRA, “denying the Jewish people their right to self-determination, eg, by claiming that the existence of a State of Israel is a racist endeavor”, is anti-Semitic, as is “drawing comparisons of contemporary Israeli policy to that of the Nazis”.

Anneliese Baldaccini of Amnesty International Italy said the bill, if adopted, would apply across schools, universities, social platforms and cultural associations.

The proposed law is “based on a definition that censors political criticism”, she said.

Activists argue that existing legislation already provides the tools to combat hate crimes.

They are instead calling for the adoption of the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism, a non-binding set of guidelines that seeks to combat anti-Semitism while protecting freedom of expression that was developed in response to the IHRA definition.

Speaking to Al Jazeera, Francesca Albanese, the Italian legal scholar and UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the occupied Palestinian territory, said legislation equating criticism of a state with anti-Semitism risked restricting freedom of expression.

“Any piece of legislation that directly or indirectly equates criticism of a state with anti-Semitism is problematic and risks creating more problems than it seeks to solve,” Albanese said.

She argued that the bill could limit the ability to analyse, document and criticise the “apartheid state of Israel”, and accused Italy of prioritising the protection of Israel over accountability.

“The need to protect the State of Israel from criticism is stronger than the need to do justice,” she said. “It is extremely dangerous because every Jewish person in the world risks being seen as a kind of emissary of Israel.”

She described Italy, under the current government, as one of Europe’s strongest defenders of Israel.

Tony La Piccirella, a Palestine solidarity activist who was part of the Global Sumud Flotilla , said he worried that the bill “provides a legal instrument to attack newsrooms, online information platforms and social media, in order to silence anyone who denounces the genocide and the entire economic system that sustains it”.

But the legislation has received strong backing from Italy’s Jewish institutional leadership.

Noemi Di Segni, president of the Union of Italian Jewish Communities (UCEI), was heard by the Senate’s Constitutional Affairs Committee in January and described legislative action against anti-Semitism as “urgent and unavoidable”.

Di Segni, who was born in Jerusalem and has served in the Israeli military, has repeatedly rejected describing Israel’s war in Gaza as genocide.

In January 2025, she called such accusations “unacceptable”, arguing that terms including “genocide”, “concentration camp”, “starve”, “Nazi” and “apartheid” should not be used to describe Israel’s conduct.

The bill has exposed divisions that cut across the government-opposition divide.

It was approved by the Senate by a large majority that included much of the opposition. Six Democratic Party senators voted in favour, while the party as a whole abstained, and those divisions have continued in the Chamber.

Among the bill’s most outspoken opponents is Stefania Ascari, of the Five Star Movement, who addressed protesters before entering parliament.

“The greatest danger to Jews and to the entire world is the terrorist state of Israel,” Ascari said. She accused the bill of targeting “freedom of expression, the autonomy of universities, [and] the work of associations and NGOs”.

The committee’s sitting ended without a vote or substantive examination.

Its work is expected to resume next week, although the timetable remains uncertain. The Chamber has scheduled a final plenary vote for October 2, leaving parliament a narrow window to complete the committee stage.

In the meantime, activists say they will continue to gather outside parliament and on the streets, to vent their concerns.

articles.title: For 'horrible moment,' Bush White House thought US military shot down Flight 93
articles.summary: Condoleezza Rice recalled the tense moment she and George W. Bush believed Flight 93 had been shot down while coordinating responses in a bunker.
articles.body: Former President George W. Bush discussed his memories of 9/11 with his former secretary of state, Condoleezza Rice, ahead of the 25th anniversary of the attacks this week. Bush and Rice said they both remember sitting in a bunker in the hours after the attacks, coordinating the U.S. domestic response. Rice recounted how they were working to ground civilian flights across the country and said at one point they thought the U.S. military had shot down United Airlines Flight 93. "I do want to say one thing to Gen. [Daniel] Caine, because something in what you said, our paths crossed in a strange way. So you mentioned that you heard that as the president, you have to understand the hard decisions that this man had to make, just like that. And one of them was what would happen if a plane was not properly identifying itself, because every plane had become a missile," Rice said. FLIGHT 93 HERO'S DAD WARNS 'ENEMIES FROM WITHIN' AIM TO DESTROY AMERICA AT THE BALLOT BOX "And so we were trying to land, I remember Norm Mineta, the transportation secretary, trying to land planes on a legal pad, yellow pad, legal pad. But you'd given the order through the vice president that should a plane not squawk properly, it should be shot down. Gen. Caine, we thought initially, standing in that bunker, that Flight 93 had been shot down," she continued. 9/11 MUSEUM UNVEILS EXHIBITION FOR GENERATION TOO YOUNG TO REMEMBER THE ATTACKS: 'CALLED EVERYBODY TO LEAD' "Yeah, I thought it was the same thing," Bush said. "And there was this horrible moment where the vice president kept trying to get confirmation as to what had happened. And for about 10 minutes we thought we'd shot down a civilian aircraft. And that always, to me, represented just how hard the decisions were that you had to take under a lot of pressure," Rice said. The event, called, "A Legacy of Service: America at the 25th Anniversary of 9/11," saw Bush host many members of his 2001 administration in Texas. articles.title: Talarico touts GOP support for Senate campaign
articles.summary: Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico on Thursday touted endorsements from 21 current and former Republican officials and party leaders ahead of his November faceoff against state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R). The endorsements come from former members of Congress, Texas state lawmakers and other officials, with several citing Paxton directly as their reason for…
articles.body:
Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico on Thursday touted endorsements from 21 current and former Republican officials and party leaders ahead of his November faceoff against state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R).

The endorsements come from former members of Congress, Texas state lawmakers and other officials, with several citing Paxton directly as their reason for crossing party lines.

“As a Republican, I believe in faith, family, the rule of law, and holding public officials accountable when they betray the public trust,” Bryan City Council member and Mayor Pro Tem James Edge (R) said in a statement. “I will support plenty of Republicans this November, but I cannot vote for Ken Paxton.”

The group, dubbed Republicans for Talarico, includes former Dallas Mayor Steve Bartlett, former Rep. Adam Kinzinger (R-Ill.) and retired Texas Supreme Court Chief Justice Tom Phillips.

“I’m proud to welcome Republicans into this campaign to take power back for working people — because the real fight in this country is not left versus right, it’s top versus bottom,” Talarico said in a statement announcing the endorsements.

One of the founding members of the group is David Maxwell, a former Texas Ranger who served as director of law enforcement in Paxton’s attorney general office. He was one of the senior officials who reported Paxton to the FBI in 2020, accusing him of bribery and abuse of office.

Paxton was later impeached in 2023 in the state House, though he was later acquitted by the Texas Senate.

The cross-party endorsements come as the key Senate race draws increased national attention and spending. MAGA Inc., the political group aligned with President Trump, recently launched a $10 million television ad buy to support Paxton in the race.

Democrats have not held a Senate seat in Texas in decades. But polling shows Talarico, who recently said he does not support transgender athletes playing in girls’ sports if it is not safe or fair, has a solid chance of flipping the seat for the party, and the nonpartisan Cook Political Report has rated the race as a toss-up.

articles.title: We are sliding toward war — and not the one we’re already in
articles.summary: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi warns that the ongoing war with Iran is depleting critical U.S. weapon stockpiles and diverting military resources away from the Indo-Pacific, thereby weakening deterrence against China.
articles.body:
Wars are measured not only by what they cost today, but by the risks they leave behind.

Eighteen American service members have been killed and 790 wounded in President Trump’s illegal and unconstitutional war with Iran. Military families have been forever changed, and the Pentagon estimates major war costs will reach $37.5 billion by the end of this fiscal year . More than six months after President Trump began a war he suggested would be short, the United States and Iran are still trading major strikes , with no diplomatic end in sight.

Fighting around the Strait of Hormuz has driven up energy, shipping and food costs. Every day President Trump fails to secure a diplomatic end to this war, those costs will continue to mount.

But the greater danger is what this war is doing to American deterrence.

Eight decades ago, military strategist Bernard Brodie wrote , “Thus far the chief purpose of our military establishment has been to win wars. From now on its chief purpose must be to avert them.”

Americans understandably want to stay out of wars. The best way to do that is to maintain the capability and resolve that convince our adversaries aggression will fail. President Trump’s war with Iran is weakening that deterrence by consuming many of the weapons the United States needs to deter aggression by the Chinese Communist Party.

Defense planners call these stockpiles our “magazine depth,” and we are draining them faster than we can rebuild them.

The United States has reportedly burned through almost half of its global supply of Tomahawk cruise missiles and used “ virtually all” of its Army Tactical Missile Systems and Precision Strike Missiles . By mid-July, U.S. forces had also fired roughly 1,700 Patriot and more than 200 THAAD interceptors .

Those numbers matter because a conflict with China would consume enormous quantities of the same weapons. In simulations conducted by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, U.S. forces generally expended 5,000 long-range missiles in just four weeks of conflict with China .

The Pentagon is racing to increase production, signing seven-year agreements intended to triple Patriot PAC-3 MSE production capacity and quadruple THAAD production capacity.

That’s necessary. But seven-year agreements will not refill our magazines tomorrow. Funding can move quickly. Production cannot.

During my recent visit to Ukraine, I saw how Ukrainians have adapted to missile and drone warfare, electronic warfare, and the challenge of sustaining weapons production under attack. We should learn from their experience and expand weapons co-production with Ukraine and our allies to help rebuild the industrial capacity and stockpiles we need.

Our own military leaders are warning that time matters. Senior commanders have reportedly warned that prolonging large-scale operations against Iran is unsustainable and risks weakening America’s ability to confront threats elsewhere.

The consequences are already visible in the Indo-Pacific. More than 30 ships that were supposed to be in the Pacific have been sent to the Middle East , while missile-defense capabilities have also been drawn from the region and allies face possible delays in American weapons deliveries.

This is what Xi Jinping and the People’s Liberation Army are watching.

Former CIA Director William Burns said Xi directed the People’s Liberation Army to be ready to conduct a successful invasion of Taiwan by 2027 , while stressing that readiness does not mean Xi has decided to invade. Beijing can see how quickly the U.S. is exhausting critical weapons, how slowly we can replace them, and how an open-ended war in the Middle East is pulling military resources away from the Indo-Pacific.

CSIS has warned that depleted missile inventories have created a “ window of vulnerability ” for a potential Western Pacific conflict.

None of this means Xi will invade Taiwan tomorrow. That misses the point of deterrence. The danger begins when Beijing concludes that the U.S. lacks the weapons, industrial capacity, or staying power to make aggression prohibitively costly. That could make China more willing to intensify coercion, blockade or quarantine Taiwan, or test American commitments elsewhere in the region.

We must rapidly rebuild America’s magazine depth, expand weapons production and co-production with our allies, and restore the military readiness needed to deter the Chinese Communist Party.

And we must stop draining critical weapons, forces, and strategic focus into an open-ended war with Iran that is weakening our ability to prevent a far more dangerous conflict in the Pacific.

America’s objective is not to fight a war with China. It is to prevent one. That requires preserving the military capability, magazine depth, alliances, and demonstrated resolve that convince Beijing aggression will fail.

The great lesson of the past century is that the true measure of American military strength is its ability to prevent wars before they begin. Its greatest triumphs are the wars the world will never have to endure.

Raja Krishnamoorthi represents the 8th Congressional District of Illinois in the U.S. House of Representatives and is a senior member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.

articles.title: Utah governor designates Sept. 10 as ‘Charlie Kirk Day’ 1 year after assassination
articles.summary: Utah Gov. Spencer Cox announced Thursday that Sept. 10 would be known as “Charlie Kirk Day” in Utah, a year after the political commentator was assassinated in the state. “One year ago today, Charlie Kirk came to Utah to take part in a fundamental American tradition: speak openly, debate ideas, and persuade others,” he said…
articles.body:
Utah Gov. Spencer Cox announced Thursday that Sept. 10 would be known as “Charlie Kirk Day” in Utah, a year after the political commentator was assassinated in the state.

“One year ago today, Charlie Kirk came to Utah to take part in a fundamental American tradition: speak openly, debate ideas, and persuade others,” he said on social platform X . “Today, we honor Charlie’s memory by choosing a politics worthy of our country, one where we stand firmly for what we believe and reject violence.”

“September 10, 2026, is officially Charlie Kirk Day in Utah,” he concluded.

Kirk’s conservative nonprofit Turning Point USA — which was taken over by his widow, Erika Kirk — is expected to convene at Utah Valley University later Thursday to remember him.

Charlie Kirk will also be honored Thursday at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas, where President Trump said Wednesday night , “We will not let them win. And in Charlie’s honor, I just want to say we love you, Charlie.”

Kirk was killed while hosting one of his “Prove Me Wrong” debates at Utah Valley University. Tyler Robinson is on trial in the slaying on seven charges , including aggravated murder.

Utah District Judge Tony Graf approved the aggravated murder charge , which under state law makes Robinson eligible for the death penalty. In the state of Utah, aggravated murder must involve at least one “ statutory aggravating factor ” — such as the defendant holding previous violent crime convictions or in cases of the killing of a minor.

In Robinson’s case, prosecutors accused the shooter of posing “a great risk of death” to others, an eligible statutory factor, during Kirk’s killing.

articles.title: El-Sayed hits Rogers on GOP convention appearance in new online game
articles.summary: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is trolling his Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), over his appearance at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas via a video game. The retro-style game’s start screen features the game’s title — Come Home, Mike — and Rogers’s face superimposed on a cartoon body standing on a…
articles.body:
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is trolling his Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), over his appearance at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas via a video game.

The retro-style game’s start screen features the game’s title — Come Home, Mike — and Rogers’s face superimposed on a cartoon body standing on a boat in water.

“Help Mike Rogers find his way from Florida back to Michigan,” text on the start screen reads. “(He hasn’t managed it yet).”

Below the start button, instructions tell the player to “drag Mike’s yacht” and “answer three questions to unlock the doors home.”

Once the game begins, the player starts out in Cape Coral, Fla., shown as a pixelated sandy beach with a palm tree. Those playing the game have to direct Rogers, on his boat, through a maze on water to get to a football field in Michigan.

Football has become a contentious issue in the race , with Rogers accusing El-Sayed of being against the sport and El-Sayed challenging Rogers to a tackle football game in lieu of a debate, which he claims Rogers is ducking.

El-Sayed has slammed Rogers before for moving to Florida after leaving the House, telling the former representative “if you want to be a Florida man, go be a Florida man” last month.

In the video game, Rogers and occasionally his boat hit a roadblock where the player is forced to make a choice between a “yes” and “no” option. However, the “yes” option is never actually available.

“Mike, Michiganders are really struggling with the cost of prescription drugs,” one of the roadblock prompts reads. “Will you agree to vote to lower prescription drug prices when you get to the Senate?”

After the last roadblock, access to the “Michigan” end point is restricted, and the player is directed to the midterm convention in Dallas.

Rogers is speaking at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday evening, while other Republicans in contentious Senate races are skipping the event amid Trump’s slumping approval ratings, the ongoing Iran war and Democrats’ recent surge in the generic congressional ballot.

The Hill has reached out to the Rogers campaign for comment.

articles.title: Zohran Mamdani urged to skip New York City's 9/11 memorial: 'Vile antisemite'
articles.summary: Rep. Mike Lawler demands Zohran Mamdani skip the 9/11 memorial, citing the NYC mayor's ties to terror sympathizers and antisemitic rhetoric.
articles.body: DALLAS – A House Republican representing the New York City suburbs is calling on Mayor Zohran Mamdani to skip the Sept. 11 memorial in downtown Manhattan. "From my vantage point, I don't think he should be there, and I think most New Yorkers agree that he should not be there," Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., told Fox News and Fox News Digital. "Certainly, the 9/11 families and the first responders believe he should not be there." Political rancor is threatening to cast a long shadow over this year's Sept. 11 remembrance events, marking 25 years since the tragedy that rocked the United States. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's past rhetoric and links to terror sympathizers are spurring intense backlash ahead of the city's events memorializing the World Trade Center attacks, with Republicans and people whose lives were changed by the attacks demanding he not show his face. If you go look at many of the people that support his administration, they agree with that rhetoric. They agree with that philosophy," Lawler said. Republican Study Committee Chairman August Pfluger, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital that Mamdani should not attend Sept. 11 memorial events "until he can... actually call out terror groups around the world for what they want to do to this country, and that includes Hamas."
