articles.title: Trump invokes Charlie Kirk at RNC convention
articles.summary: 💸 Plus: Who wants $5K? {beacon} It’s Thursday, and the 49ers play the Rams tonight. May the best Californians win. In today’s issue: TPUSA without Charlie Kirk Fetterman friction Trump’s $5K promise to Americans Strait of Hormuz hostilities Programming note: We’re Abigail Walker and Claire Leibowitz filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and…
articles.body:
It’s Thursday, and the 49ers play the Rams tonight. May the best Californians win.

Programming note : We’re Abigail Walker and Claire Leibowitz filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to awalker@thehill.com and cleibowitz@thehill.com .

Thursday marks one year since conservative activist and leader of Turning Point USA (TPUSA) Charlie Kirk was assassinated at Utah Valley University (UVU).

Utah Gov. Spencer Cox (R) declared Sept. 10 Charlie Kirk Day in Utah and said moments of tragedy should not deepen divisions, but rather foster empathy.

Kirk was a well-known debater who went toe-to-toe with college students, liberals and occasionally public figures in a “Prove Me Wrong” format that allowed anyone to walk up to his table and discuss topics including immigration, race and social issues.

TPUSA is one of the most dominant youth-oriented conservative groups in the country, with chapters spread across U.S. universities. It also received extra chops after President Trump and Vice President Vance credited Kirk and the organization for electoral victories.

Although his wife, Erika Kirk , took over the nonprofit after his death, TPUSA is still left with a void that is difficult to fill, The Hill’s Caroline Vakil reports.

Could the next Charlie Kirk be like Forrest Gump?: Blake Neff, another conservative activist who worked with Kirk, has taken over the radio program the “Charlie Kirk Show.”

He describes himself as being like Forrest Gump, Politico reports , because he was a little-known figure who was pushed, with luck and pluckiness, toward the center of many important moments for conservatives.

He shares Kirk’s values and aims to host healthy debate about conservative tenets without censoring or cancelling his opponents to silence them.

Trump and TPUSA: Trump called Kirk “a great friend” at Wednesday night’s Republican National Committee midterm convention in Dallas.

The president tied together his opponents and Kirk’s demise, saying “the mask came off the radical left” as people cheered Kirk’s death.

“Those same people are trying to get power over you in this election, and they’re all voting Democrat,” he added. “We will not let them win, in Charlie’s honor.”

Trump shouted out Erika Kirk, who was in attendance and received applause from the audience, along with chants of “Charlie.” She is set to speak Thursday night.

Memorial maelstrom: TPUSA is hosting a memorial Thursday night at UVU, which has once again split the campus, per the New York Times . While some students welcome the opportunity to honor Kirk, others, including those in the chapter of Students for a Democratic Society, are planning a protest outside the memorial.

“This is almost like making this a holiday,” Ethan Cunningham, the president of the campus Students for a Democratic Society, told the Times.

The university president also told the outlet that he is planning to attend the memorial and the protest to show that the university can foster dialogues on both sides.

The university canceled classes and ramped up security.

Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) made a video appearance at the RNC’s first midterm convention, stirring the partisan pot.

“Why am I here talking to you today? Because, well, I’m a commonsense Democrat,” the lawmaker said in introducing his Pennsylvania colleague, Sen. Dave McCormick (R). He then criticized the Democratic Party’s leftist flank, calling socialism an “anti-American way of life.”

Commentator Stephen A. Smith , when asked about Fetterman’s RNC appearance, told NewsNation host Chris Cuomo that while it’s one thing to reject socialism, “It’s another thing entirely to be a Democrat and be a part of a hype video at a Republican convention.”

“That is just pretty much spitting in the face of Democrats who elected you to office,” Smith added.

Bill O’Reilly also spoke with Cuomo about Fetterman gracing the RNC. The former Fox News host predicted the senator “is going to be a Republican,” a switch that might threaten potential Democratic control of the Senate come November.

Fetterman has frequently criticized his party in recent months, typically citing democratic socialism and a diminished support of Israel as reasons for his growing distaste for Democrats.

Trump announced at the RNC convention that should Republicans maintain control of Congress, American adults would each receive $5,000 .

The president’s promise begs many questions. As The Hill’s Mallory Wilson wrote: “The legality of this disbursal is unclear. There are about 270 million adults in the U.S.”

Trump said the proposed payouts would be possible “because we’ve done so well and because our country is making so much money.”

Totally not controversial : Vance late Wednesday night defended the president’s dividend promise on Fox News. Host Bret Baier said critics would label the payout, which would amount to around $1.3 trillion, as “bribing voters.”

Like Trump, the vice president responded that the Trump administration was “taking an extraordinary amount of revenue,” pointing to recent tariffs as a source of so much cash.

“If you keep us in power and allow us to continue to do these things, then you’re going to share in some of the benefit of this incredible wealth that we’re creating in the United States of America,” Vance added. “I don’t think it’s a controversial idea.”

Hostilities in the Middle East have heightened in recent days, with the Islamic Republic increasing its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.

“Iran is escalating because they don’t see other options,” Marc Sievers, the former U.S. ambassador to Oman, told The Wall Street Journal . “They’re under tremendous pressure from the blockade and the new sanctions.”

In a conflict first, the Islamic Republic launched missiles directly at American naval ships and aircraft carriers.

According to U.S. Central Command, the warships thwarted the strikes, which, if successful, the Journal posited “would almost certainly trigger a fierce U.S. response and risk reigniting a full-scale war.”

Meanwhile in Jordan , Iranian forces between Tuesday night and Wednesday morning local time struck multiple U.S. aircraft at the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, individuals with direct knowledge of the situation told CBS news .

One A-10 Thunderbolt and eight F-15s were among the damaged aircraft, according to the anonymous sources.

Didn’t happen : In a phone call with NewsNation’s Robert Sherman on Thursday, the president denied any damage to U.S. aircraft.

“None whatsoever. No damage. No nothing,” Trump told Sherman.

ABC late-night comedian Jimmy Kimmel said an interview he conducted with Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico will not air on broadcast because of what he called threats issued to his network by President Trump’s Federal Communications Commission (FCC).

Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins (R) is appearing before the state Supreme Court on Thursday as judges weigh whether to hold him in contempt amid an escalating battle over the state’s congressional map.

Talarico in a Wednesday interview with Fox News expressed his qualified opposition to transgender athletes playing in girls’ sports, saying such athletes should not be allowed to play if it is not fair or safe.

articles.title: Can Trump really pay $5,000 to every American adult?
articles.summary: Analysts question if the US president's election year offer is workable, legal or affordable.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has offered every adult American $5,000 (£3,700) if Republicans win November's midterm elections, but it is unclear how such a plan would be funded and whether it is legal.

His remarks prompted raucous applause from supporters at a party convention on Wednesday night, but Democrats labelled it an "empty promise".

Trump also told the Republican conference that the money would have to be spent in the US, but it is unclear how that would be monitored.

The US president has given no details on how it would be funded, though Vice-President JD Vance suggested it might be paid for by tariff revenue and that such cheques would not go to wealthy Americans.

Under US federal law, it is illegal to give payments that are intended to influence the way a person is voting.

However, some experts have said the offer made by Trump in Texas on Wednesday could be seen as a pledge to cut taxes, which is legal.

Dr Joan Mahoney, lecturer in law at the University of Southampton, told the BBC she thought the offer would be legal as it would be similar to a campaign promise - though she said politicians "don't usually do it quite this explicitly".

"On the one hand it sounds a bit like a bribe, vote for the Republicans and you'll get money, which would be decidedly illegal," she said.

"But on the other hand it would go to everyone, regardless of how they voted so it isn't in that sense a bribe.

"I think it would be legal. It's the same kind of campaign pledge as saying 'if my party wins we'll reduce taxes'. Every party does that all the time... and that's obviously perfectly legal."

However, Laurel Rapp, director of the US and North America programme at Chatham House, told the BBC that Trump's offer seemed to be "a very different, very transactional agreement" from the kind of promise usually made by candidates in an election period.

Aside from the question of legality, some have also asked whether Trump's offer would be feasible financially in the context of increasing US debt, partially as a result of the war in Iran.

There are nearly 270 million American adults, meaning a $5,000 payout would cost the US government some $1.3 trillion.

Trump gave no details on how such cheques would be funded.

Congress authorises spending in the US, but the president did not say whether he planned to ask for legislative approval for any payments.

And legal experts said it was unlikely he could approve such a vast sum via a presidential executive order.

Erica York, a senior economist at the Washington DC-based Tax Foundation, told the BBC she would be "extremely surprised" if Congress approved any proposal.

"This would be one of the worst ways to use $1.3 trillion," she said.

"We're on a very unsustainable track, with deficits only projected to grow and grow," York added.

Speaking to Fox News after Trump's speech, Vice-President Vance indicated that the payments could be funded by money raised by the president from tariffs.

However, such revenue to date falls far short of the money that would be needed to account for Trump's $5,000 cheques offer.

According to the Bipartisan Policy Center, the US has brought in around $475bn in tariff and excise tax revenue since the beginning of 2025.

But more than $100bn has been refunded after the Supreme Court struck down many tariffs earlier this year.

When asked how the payouts could work, the White House said in a statement to the BBC: "The doomers and naysayers have consistently doubted President Trump."

"With the continued support of the American people, President Trump will keep delivering real results," added spokesman Davis Ingle.

Trump says every adult American will get $5,000 if Republicans win midterms

Four key takeaways from Republican midterms convention

Watch: Do Republicans blame Trump for high oil prices?

One former Republican strategist and pollster said Trump's latest offer should be firmly seen in the context of an election that is now less than two months away.

"It is an extraordinary promise, and I'm not sure where that money is going to come from - but it is campaign season," Robert Moran told the BBC.

Chatham House's Rapp said Trump was thinking short term to try to keep hold of Congress as he enters the final two years of his term in office.

"Money is something that he is now resorting to because the polling is not looking good for Republicans and the polling is not looking good for him," she continued.

Trump has previously proposed $2,000 cheques to be funded by tariff revenues, but those payouts have not materialised.

Former President Joe Biden was accused of buying votes when he promised $2,000 Covid stimulus cheques for Americans if two Democratic candidates in Georgia would win election to the US Senate in January 2021.

A similar issue of legality came to the fore ahead of the 2024 presidential election, during which billionaire Trump supporter Elon Musk offered cash incentives to registered voters in seven swing states who signed a certain petition.

Additional reporting by Bernd Debusmann Jr, White House reporter

articles.summary: Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.) didn’t mince words about Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and his video appearance at Republicans’ midterm convention, calling it a “stunt” that she said was “gravely disappointing.” “I will tell you from the ground from suburban Philadelphia, my constituents are livid,” Dean told reporters at House Democratic event responding to the GOP convention on…
articles.body:
Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.) didn’t mince words about Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and his video appearance at Republicans’ midterm convention, calling it a “stunt” that she said was “gravely disappointing.”

“I will tell you from the ground from suburban Philadelphia, my constituents are livid,” Dean told reporters at House Democratic event responding to the GOP convention on Thursday. “Those who went out and knocked doors for him — they are absolutely livid.”

Fetterman shocked his party on Wednesday when he appeared in a video during the GOP midterm convention before Sen. Dave McCormick’s (R-Pa.) remarks, lauding the GOP senator and calling him a “friend.”

“Why am I here talking to you today?” Fetterman said the prerecorded video. “Because, well, I’m a commonsense Democrat.”

“David McCormick is the kind of senator that gets the job done,” the Pennsylvania Democrat said while vowing that he and McCormick would work with Trump to protect the state’s steel industry.

Fetterman has increasingly isolated himself from his own party – a far cry from the staunch progressive he positioned himself as when he ran for the Senate seat in 2022.

The Wall Street Journal recently reported that Fetterman has shown little interest in meeting with some of his constituent groups, including a children’s hospital in Philadelphia regarding their concerns over Medicaid cuts and vaccines. Instead, sources told the news outlet that the Democratic senator has reportedly been more interested in Israel advocacy efforts and meeting with conservative media.

Fetterman has suggested that the moment requires him to be bipartisan, but his antics have started to frustrate members of his party.

“I got to know and really like him and his family and his values,” Dean said, noting she briefly ran against him in 2018 for Pennsylvania lieutenant governor.

“But what we have seen in his service as a senator is something very different than when I got to know around John,” she continued. “We can see in his work ethic that he’s just not present. He doesn’t participate much at all in his own committees, let alone attend them.”

articles.title: Missouri judges press state on map plans after Supreme Court ruling
articles.summary: Missouri’s top judges pressed the state on Thursday over how it will revert to an old congressional map after the Supreme Court blocked officials from implementing their new, GOP-favored lines. That block landed moments before a hearing on whether Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins should be held in contempt for directing local officials to proceed with the design, which would have…
articles.body:
Missouri’s top judges pressed the state on Thursday over how it will revert to an old congressional map after the Supreme Court blocked officials from implementing their new, GOP-favored lines.

That block landed moments before a hearing on whether Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins should be held in contempt for directing local officials to proceed with the design, which would have given the GOP a 7-1 advantage in its House delegation.

“We just want to make sure that the law is followed,” said Chief Justice W. Brent Powell.

The hearing reflected the chaotic nature of Missouri’s redistricting battle after a barrage of recent legal rulings. The parties were still processing the Supreme Court’s latest decision when arguments kicked off in the state. It left the judges and lawyers alike scrambling to figure out what comes next.

Principal Deputy Solicitor General William Seidleck tried to assuage concerns, but he cautioned the state was still “carefully evaluating the situation.”

“I want to make sure that we’re all on the same page here. HB-1 never went into effect, right?” Powell pushed him shortly into the argument, referring to Republicans’ favored map.

“Yes, per this court’s holding,” Seidleck conceded.

Still, the judges appeared concerned. Powell warned Hoskins “to not venture far” until the contempt push is resolved. At another point, Judge Paul Wilson quipped, “it’s just English” as he scoffed at the state’s responses.

The court has announced it will reconvene Thursday afternoon for another session.

Missouri’s election plunged into chaos last week when the state’s top court ruled a referendum needed to take place before Republicans can implement their favored 7-1 congressional map . A federal judge then separately told officials they needed to move ahead with the map anyways, because that’s what was used for the primary.

The dueling directives led to public confusion about what would happen for the midterms, now less than 60 days away.

“The secretary was truly in a rock and a hard place,” Seidleck said.

Less than an hour before Thursday’s hearing, the Supreme Court lifted the latter order. The state’s deputy solicitor general agreed that changed things.

“This court’s injunction is now fully controlling the situation,” Seidleck continued, “And unless and until a federal court comes back and says otherwise, it’s this court’s injunction that is guiding the analysis right now.”

That answer did not seem to completely satisfy the Missouri judges.

“But you would agree again – I’m just going to reiterate this: That federal guidance that you potentially could get down the road is not going to change the fact that HB-1 never went into effect,” Powell said.
